# Model Results

> Part 1 = regression (biomarker levels). Part 2 = calibrated risk classification.

**Data:** NHANES 2013–2018 (CDC, public domain) — 17,961 adults aged 18+ across three survey cycles.
**Model:** `HistGradientBoostingRegressor`, one per target, 16 features.
**Generated by:** `python -m src.training.train_risk_engine` → `reports/nhanes_metrics.json`

---

## 1. Headline

| Target | Unit | n (train) | MAE | Baseline MAE | Gain | R² *(cycle holdout)* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **systolic_bp** | mmHg | 9,921 | 12.73 | 15.25 | **+16.5%** | **+0.270** |
| **diastolic_bp** | mmHg | 9,849 | 8.83 | 9.55 | +7.5% | +0.089 |
| **hba1c** | % | 9,834 | 0.58 | 0.64 | +9.2% | **+0.129** |
| **triglycerides** | mg/dL | 4,525 | 47.10 | 54.07 | +12.9% | +0.045 |
| **ggt** | U/L | 9,693 | 16.35 | 18.58 | +12.0% | −0.001 |
| **fli** | 0–100 | 4,293 | 8.93 | 29.29 | +69.5% | +0.852 |

All six beat a mean-predictor baseline on **both** a random split and a cycle holdout (train 2013–2016 → test 2017–2018). The cycle holdout is reported above because it is the harder, more deployment-relevant question: does this survive a survey wave collected years later?

---

## 2. The FLI number needs an asterisk

R² 0.852 for the Fatty Liver Index looks like the headline result. It is not what it appears, and reporting it without this section would be misleading.

FLI is a formula: `0.953·ln(TG) + 0.139·BMI + 0.718·ln(GGT) + 0.053·waist − 15.745`. Two of its four terms — **BMI and waist — are inputs we measure exactly**, not quantities the model estimates. So most of the variance is arithmetic, not learning.

Ablation on the same held-out split:

| Approach | MAE | R² |
|---|---|---|
| Mean predictor | 29.78 | 0.000 |
| **Bedogni formula + cohort-median TG/GGT — no ML at all** | **9.32** | **+0.843** |
| Gradient boosting on `bmi` + `waist_cm` only | 9.03 | +0.849 |
| Gradient boosting on all 16 features | **8.71** | **+0.860** |

**84.3% of FLI variance is explained with no machine learning whatsoever.** The model earns a further **+6.1% MAE reduction** over that — real, but modest.

The training code therefore judges FLI against the formula reference, not the mean predictor, and `test_fli_is_judged_against_the_formula_reference` enforces it.

---

## 3. What the model is and is not good at

**Genuinely useful — hypertension and dysglycaemia.** Systolic BP (R² 0.270) and HbA1c (R² 0.129) are the strongest honest results. These are the two conditions the project pitched but v1 never implemented at all.

**Weak — triglycerides.** R² 0.045. MAE improves 12.9% over the baseline, so the ranking carries some signal, but the model explains almost none of the variance. Serum triglycerides swing with recent meals and fasting state; a single 24-hour dietary recall cannot capture that.

**Effectively unpredictable — GGT.** R² −0.001 on the cycle holdout. MAE improves 12.0%, which reflects the log-transform pulling predictions toward the median rather than any real skill. GGT is driven by alcohol, medications, genetics and hepatic pathology — mostly things this feature set does not observe. **This is a negative result and it is reported as one.**

Because FLI depends on TG and GGT, its direct prediction is doing well *despite* its components, not because of them. That is exactly why predicting it directly beats composing it (R² 0.86 vs ~0.05).

---

## 4. Feature importance

Permutation importance (MAE damage when a column is shuffled):

| Target | Top contributors |
|---|---|
| fli | **waist_cm (+18.00)**, bmi (+7.83), age (+0.85), fat_g (+0.75) |
| systolic_bp | **age (+4.34)**, bmi (+0.60), sex_male (+0.50), energy_kcal (+0.42) |
| triglycerides | **waist_cm (+6.18)**, fat_g (+3.48), age (+2.51), bmi (+2.20) |
| diastolic_bp | age (+1.61), sex_male (+0.25), waist_cm (+0.25), bmi (+0.21) |
| ggt | energy_kcal (+1.23), age (+0.87), sex_male (+0.84), fat_g (+0.61) |
| hba1c | **age (+0.13)**, waist_cm (+0.04), energy_kcal (+0.03), sugar_g (+0.02) |

**Waist circumference is the single most valuable input across the board** — more than BMI, in every case where both appear. That is a concrete, actionable product conclusion: onboarding should insist on a waist measurement rather than treating it as optional.

---

## 5. Why the previous model was replaced

The v1 multimodal LSTM+MLP reported **R² 0.900 (TG) / 0.974 (GGT)**. Both figures were artifacts.

| | |
|---|---|
| Leak 1 | `MinMaxScaler.fit_transform` ran on all 5,475 rows **before** the train/test split |
| Leak 2 | The split was random over 14-day sliding windows overlapping by **13 of 14 days**, with the same 15 users on both sides |
| Corrected | Split by **disjoint user**, scalers fit on train only → **R² −0.89 (TG) / −0.87 (GGT)** — worse than predicting the mean |

Separately, the *served* path was broken: `predict.py` concatenated a 1-row profile with a 14-row window on `axis=1`, leaving the MLP branch all-NaN. Every user received a bit-identical prediction regardless of age, BMI or diet. Verified: a healthy 20-year-old and a high-risk 73-year-old both returned `153.47 / 34.44`.

Fifteen synthetic personas is **nine training examples at the person level**. No architecture recovers from that. Hence the move to real data.

| | v1 (synthetic) | v2 (NHANES) |
|---|---|---|
| People | 15 personas | **17,961 adults** |
| Provenance | Generated, with an explicit `trend_type` label | CDC survey, public domain |
| Honest TG R² | −0.89 | +0.045 |
| Conditions | Fatty liver only | Fatty liver + dysglycaemia + hypertension |

v2's numbers are far lower and far more trustworthy.

---

## 6. Limitations

1. **US population.** NHANES is American. South Asians develop metabolic disease at lower BMI and waist thresholds, so an India-deployed model needs recalibration (planned against NFHS-5 / LASI).
2. **Cross-sectional.** One blood draw per person. The model estimates a *current* level; it cannot observe how biomarkers respond to a behaviour change over time.
3. **Triglycerides come from the fasting subsample** (4,525 usable rows against ~9,800 for the other targets).
4. **Diet is one 24-hour recall** — a single day, self-reported, not habitual intake.
5. **Sleep and activity are self-reported** in NHANES but sensor-measured in the app. The two are correlated but not identical; this instrument mismatch is unquantified.
6. **GGT is not predictable here** (§3), which caps how much the fatty-liver estimate can improve.
7. **Not a medical device.** Screening and education only. Every API response carries this disclaimer.

---

## 7. Reproduce

```bash
cd ml
python -m src.data.nhanes.download          # ~25 MB from the CDC, no registration
python -m src.data.nhanes.build_dataset     # -> data/processed/nhanes_metabolic.csv
python -m src.training.train_risk_engine    # -> models/risk_engine.joblib, reports/nhanes_metrics.json
python -m src.training.train_classifiers    # -> models/risk_classifiers.joblib, reports/shap/
python -m pytest tests/ -q                  # 48 passed
```

# Part 2 — Risk Classification (Day 3)

Part 1 estimated biomarker *levels*. This part answers the question a user
actually asks: **am I at risk?** -- as a calibrated probability.

**Generated by:** `python -m src.training.train_classifiers` -> `reports/classifier_metrics.json`, `reports/shap/`

## 8. Classification results

| Condition | Prevalence | AUROC | AUPRC | Sensitivity | Specificity | PPV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **hypertension** | 49.8% | **0.802** | 0.746 | 91% | 0.53 | 0.66 |
| **dysglycaemia** | 41.2% | **0.799** | 0.689 | 93% | 0.43 | 0.54 |
| **diabetes** | 16.9% | **0.799** | 0.383 | 90% | 0.55 | 0.29 |
| fatty_liver | 42.7% | 0.958 | 0.936 | 92% | 0.83 | 0.80 | 

Operating points target ~90% sensitivity, not accuracy. This is a screening
tool: missing an at-risk person costs more than a false alarm that resolves
with a confirmatory blood test.

**All three conditions the pitch promised now exist.** v1 shipped fatty liver
only, and even that was computed from `Math.random()` biomarkers.

## 9. The fatty-liver AUROC of 0.958 is close to a tautology

Same caveat as the regression head in section 2, and it is worth restating
because 0.958 is the number a reader will remember.

| Model | AUROC |
|---|---|
| All 16 features | 0.9577 |
| **bmi + waist_cm only** | **0.9548** |
| Gain from the other 14 features | **+0.0029** |

FLI is a formula whose four terms include BMI and waist, both of which are
measured exactly rather than predicted. The classifier is therefore mostly
restating anthropometry. SHAP agrees: `waist_cm` (3.203) and `bmi` (1.863)
dwarf everything else, the third-ranked feature scoring 0.250.

**A test enforces that this baseline stays recorded**, so the AUROC can never be
quoted bare (`test_fatty_liver_records_its_anthropometry_baseline`).

The genuinely predictive heads are hypertension, dysglycaemia and diabetes at
AUROC ~0.80.

## 10. What a flag actually means

At the screening operating point, PPV runs from 0.29 (diabetes) to 0.80
(fatty liver). For diabetes that means **roughly 7 of every 10 people flagged do
not have it**.

That is the correct trade for screening at 90% sensitivity in a 16.9%-prevalence
population, but it dictates how the result must be worded in the product: a flag
is a prompt to get tested, never a diagnosis. The API disclaimer and the
`RiskScore.rationale` text both say so.

## 11. Calibration

Isotonic regression, fitted on a held-out 20% split.

| Condition | Brier before | Brier after |
|---|---|---|
| fatty_liver | 0.0830 | 0.0817 |
| diabetes | 0.1199 | 0.1183 |
| hypertension | 0.1793 | 0.1788 |
| dysglycaemia | 0.1786 | **0.1803** (slightly worse) |

Calibration barely moved the needle, and for dysglycaemia it marginally hurt.
The honest read: the raw gradient-boosting probabilities were already close to
calibrated, so this step buys reliability rather than accuracy.

Reliability is good mid-range and **overconfident at the top**. For dysglycaemia
the 0.8-0.9 bin predicts 0.883 where only 0.636 are affected, and 0.9-1.0
predicts 0.991 against 0.775 observed. Both bins are thin (n=22 and n=49), so
this is partly sampling noise, but the practical consequence stands: **treat
very high predicted probabilities as "high risk", not as near-certainty.**
Hypertension calibrates well throughout (worst gap 0.086).

`test_calibration_is_reasonable_in_populated_bins` enforces a gap under 0.15 for
every bin with n >= 100.

## 12. Label design: treated patients count as cases

26.7% of NHANES adults take blood-pressure medication and therefore read normal.
Labelling purely on `BP >= 130/80` would have taught the model that a medicated
hypertensive is healthy -- inverting the clinical meaning for a quarter of the
positive class. The same applies to diagnosed diabetics whose HbA1c is
controlled by treatment.

Labels therefore include medication and diagnosis status:

| Condition | Label |
|---|---|
| hypertension | `BP >= 130/80` **or** on BP medication |
| dysglycaemia | `HbA1c >= 5.7` **or** diagnosed diabetes |
| diabetes | `HbA1c >= 6.5` **or** diagnosed diabetes |

Effect on prevalence: hypertension 39.4% -> 49.8%, diabetes 12.5% -> 16.9%.

Medication status is used in the **label only, never as a feature** -- it is a
proxy for the diagnosis being predicted, and including it would be leakage.

## 13. SHAP feature attribution

Mean absolute SHAP value, exact TreeExplainer attribution, in `reports/shap/`.

| Condition | Top four |
|---|---|
| fatty_liver | **waist_cm (3.203)**, bmi (1.863), fat_g (0.250), age (0.248) |
| hypertension | **age (1.255)**, waist_cm (0.256), bmi (0.214), sex_male (0.182) |
| diabetes | **age (1.141)**, waist_cm (0.551), sugar_g (0.329), bmi (0.196) |
| dysglycaemia | **age (1.069)**, bmi (0.303), waist_cm (0.272), energy_kcal (0.181) |

Two consistent conclusions, reinforcing Part 1:

1. **Age and waist circumference dominate every head.** Age is not modifiable;
   waist is. That makes waist the single most useful thing the product can ask
   for and the most useful thing it can help a user change.
2. **`sugar_g` ranks third for diabetes** -- the strongest appearance of any
   dietary variable, and a coaching hook the recommendation engine can use.

## 14. Sanity check

A deliberately low-risk profile (25y, BMI 21, waist 74, active, non-smoker)
against a deliberately high-risk one (62y, BMI 36, waist 124, sedentary,
21 drinks/week, smoker):

| Condition | Low-risk | High-risk |
|---|---|---|
| fatty_liver | 0.000 | 1.000 |
| hypertension | 0.172 | 0.855 |
| dysglycaemia | 0.078 | 0.761 |
| diabetes | 0.022 | 0.408 |

Ordered correctly in every case. A model can beat every aggregate metric and
still be clinically absurd on an individual; this is the cheapest guard against
that, and it runs at training time and again as a test.

## 15. Additional limitations (Day 3)

8. **The fatty-liver head is largely an anthropometric restatement** (section 9).
   It is retained because FLI is the accepted screening index, but it should be
   presented as "your body measurements indicate elevated risk", not as a
   discovery.
9. **High predicted probabilities are overconfident** (section 11).
10. **PPV is low for diabetes** (0.29 at the screening threshold). Product copy
    must not imply diagnosis.
11. **Medication confounds the BP labels in the other direction too**: a
    well-controlled patient is a true case with normal physiology, so the model
    is partly learning "who gets prescribed medication", which tracks healthcare
    access and is not purely biological.

# Part 3 — Composition and Trajectory (Day 4)

## 16. The most important bug found so far

While building the trajectory feature, the composed system was run over 12 weeks
of steadily *improving* behaviour (steps 3,000 -> 12,000; sleep 5.4h -> 7.6h)
across five profiles. For a mid-range profile, **hypertension risk rose**:

| profile | fatty_liver | hypertension | dysglycaemia | diabetes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| lean 30F waist 72 | -0.00 | -0.07 | -0.34 | -0.00 |
| **mid 45M waist 95** | -0.00 | **+0.79** | -0.94 | -0.37 |
| obese 52M waist 108 | -0.56 | -0.56 | -0.49 | -0.00 |
| obese+diet 52M | -0.10 | -1.44 | -0.84 | -0.05 |
| severe 60M waist 125 | -0.00 | -0.54 | -0.35 | -0.00 |

*(slope in risk points per week; negative is improving)*

Gradient boosting is free to fit non-monotonic relationships and it did. **A
coaching product cannot tell a user to exercise more and then show their risk
climbing.** Aggregate metrics were healthy throughout: AUROC 0.80, calibration
within 0.05, sanity check passing. Only walking a trajectory exposed it.

### Fix: monotonic constraints

`HistGradientBoostingClassifier` accepts per-feature monotonic constraints. Two
features have an unambiguous clinical direction:

| Feature | Constraint |
|---|---|
| `mvpa_min_week` | decreasing (more activity -> lower risk) |
| `sedentary_min_day` | increasing (more sitting -> higher risk) |

**Sleep is deliberately left unconstrained** because it is U-shaped clinically:
both too little and too much are associated with harm. Diet is likewise free.

Measured cost:

| Condition | AUROC free | AUROC constrained | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| fatty_liver | 0.9600 | 0.9606 | **+0.0005** |
| hypertension | 0.8072 | 0.8082 | **+0.0010** |
| dysglycaemia | 0.8038 | 0.8015 | -0.0023 |
| diabetes | 0.8070 | 0.8016 | -0.0053 |

After the fix, **zero conditions rise with improving behaviour across all five
profiles.** `test_improving_behaviour_never_raises_any_risk` runs this check
over four profiles and fails the build if it regresses.

This is the cheapest 0.005 AUROC ever spent.

## 17. Composition: what supplies each number

| Output | Source |
|---|---|
| Condition probability | Calibrated classifier (Part 2) |
| Biomarker levels | NHANES regression engine (Part 1) |
| Rationale and contributors | Clinical scorers |
| Trajectory | The same real model over rolling windows |
| Anything measured | User lab values override every estimate |

Each `RiskScore` carries a `basis` field (`calibrated_classifier` or
`clinical_formula`) alongside its `provenance`, so a caller can always tell not
only how trustworthy the data was but which model answered.

## 18. Trajectory without a temporal model

The deck promised a long-term risk trajectory and early warning. That is now
delivered **without any sequence model**, and that is a deliberate choice.

The v1 design trained an LSTM to map 14 days of wearable data onto same-day
biomarkers. No real dataset can supervise that, because nobody draws blood
daily. That is exactly why the original data had to be synthetic, and why the
model scored R2 -0.89 on held-out users. Retraining it as a delta model changes
the output but not the supervision problem.

**Datasets checked and rejected on Day 4:**

| Dataset | Size | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| PMData | 1.35 GB | 16 people, **no biomarkers** -- cannot supervise |
| LifeSnaps | 586 MB | 71 people, **no biomarkers** -- cannot supervise |

What works instead: the NHANES risk engine is a function of behaviour. Applying
that real, cross-sectionally-validated model to successive 14-day windows of a
user own history produces a genuine risk-over-time series, and the trend is a
least-squares fit over those points.

**The honest limitation:** this measures how risk responds to observed behaviour
change, using a model fitted *across* people rather than *within* one. It is a
trajectory of estimates, not a forecast of individual biology.

The trajectory abstains rather than extrapolating: fewer than 14 days yields no
trajectory at all, and fewer than 3 windows yields `slope_per_week: null` with
direction `unknown`.

## 19. Additional limitations (Day 4)

12. **Trajectories are driven by wearable change only.** The profile (waist,
    weight, diet) is held constant across the window walk, so a trajectory
    understates improvement for a user who is also losing weight. Fixing this
    needs historical profile snapshots, which the backend does not yet store.
13. **Only two features are monotonically constrained.** Diet features remain
    free and could in principle show the same inverted behaviour; they were not
    constrained because the clinical direction of, for example, total fat is
    genuinely ambiguous.
14. **The synthetic LSTM is retired from the serving path** but still exists in
    `src/inference/predictor.py` for comparison. Anything it touches is tagged
    `Provenance.SIMULATION`.
